Question: What is the tax benefit if I purchase a house in May 2023, take a loan, repay it in 1.2 years, then buy a new property in my husband's name with a new loan? Can I still get a tax benefit on the interest?
Answer: This all depends upon who the home loan borrower is. The actual owner of the property matters less. The borrower can avail of the income tax benefits. Case 1: First home loan, loan taken in the name of the wife; property in the names of wife or husband or both (husband and wife) All tax benefits - till they are available - can be claimed by the wife in her ITR. Case 2: First home loan, loan taken in the name of the wife and husband; property in the names of wife or husband or both (husband and wife) All tax benefits - till they are available - can be claimed by the wife and wife in their ITR as per the ownership proportion declared in the returns. Note that the wife may be paying 100% or 75% or 0%, but in the tax return, they can declare 50–50 ownership and claim benefits in the same proportion. The proportion can be split in any manner. When the first loan is paid off (earlier), the tax benefits will stop next year. After that, if a new property is purchased and a new loan is taken, the same rules as described above will apply.

Question: As both the first and second phases of the 2024 general election saw the lowest percentage of votes poll, is it a clear indication that the opposition alliance is going to lose both phases?
Answer: History of elections has proven that when voting turnout is very high, there is a massive pro or anti-incumbency wave, generally the latter. Conversely, if the voter turnout is lesser than usual, it means one of the following: * They think that there is no point voting; their vote is inconsequential * Supporters of one side/party believe that the other side is going to win anyway; so why go out in the strong Sun and suffer discomfort? (This would be thoughts of the INDI supporters) * Supporters of one side/party believe that their side is going to win anyway; so why go out in the strong Sun and suffer discomfort? (This would be thoughts of the NDA supporters) Both the above possibilities exist. The voter % drop has been 3% to 9%. It could be that the voters who failed to vote are equally divided across both camps. If so, NDA wins. If the entire drop is on INDI voter side, then too NDA wins. Unless the drop is a massive 8% against NDA, then it becomes interesting.

Question: Has anyone accumulated 1 cr or more in mutual funds? If yes, how do you redeem the amount so you pay the least amount of LTCG?
Answer: I can understand that you wish to reduce the taxes. If your ₹1 Cr is in equity mutual funds, vested more than 365 days before, then any redemption amount qualifies as per LTCG rules. You get an exemption of ₹ 1 lakh on the gross LTCG and the rest is taxed at 10.4% (10% tax, 4% cess). To effectively pay zero tax, then if you redeem just so much that your gain is ₹1 lakh or less, there is no tax to pay. Question: I have 3 credit cards and I used cards to pay for my friends spends and they transfer that amount in my bank account and I pay my credit card bill. Does it attract to a notice from income tax?
Answer: No. The income tax will not send you a notice as long as the amounts don't cross a barrier big enough to be noticed. But let me WARN YOU (please note the bold caps) that you are treading in very treacherous swamps or a quicksand. First of all, the taxman may completely disregard that these deposits in your bank account are refunds of expenses you incurred on behalf of your friends. One or two such deposits maybe be ok. Not if they are very frequent. If the total deposits from all your friends exceed ₹50,000, the whole amount can be inferred as gift and subject to gift tax. But you may still escape that scrutiny if your income is below taxable limit. The greater danger is that a the owner of the credit cards and the person using the credit card for spending, you are responsible for the payments. If your friends fail to refunds you, you will have to take the hit. Worse still, if you fail to pay, you will be slapped with late fee, 36%++ interest and credit rating struck down. I have seen this happen. Someone sent me a message asking my advice on what to do. (Claimed that he spent ₹4.5 lakhs in friend's father's hospital bill and now friend is unable to repay. Maybe a true story but nevertheless a sorry story.) I repeat a very favourite dialogue of mine from The Godfather Part III: Friendship and money! Oil and water. - Michael Corleone to Archbishop Gilday

Question: How do I save electricity with an inverter AC?
Answer: Compared to traditional non-inverter ACs, inverter-based ACs do save electricity. The compressor is the main unit that consumes about 90% of the electricity. The rest is used by the blower/fan, the louvre swing motors, etc. The inverter in the AC is the device that regulates the compressor on/off along with the feedback from the temperature sensor. The less frequently the compressor operates, the lesser is the electricity usage. In a non-inverter AC, the compressor o/off is strictly controlled by the temperature sensor.
